absent: Bodies and contracts of default helpers for per-field and whole-CPU fetch when generic timing is disabled.
Definitions of elapsed-time reader, steal accounting, interrupt-time and other-time helpers, and tick duration constant.
Numeric encodings of virtual-time states and CPU usage categories.
Full layouts of task, runqueue, root domain, and deadline bandwidth structures beyond fields touched here.
Bandwidth arithmetic for reservation add and subtract and running versus total portions and admission-control policy.
Topology and capacity-index lookup details and per-CPU mask allocation.
Sleep-time microsecond helper implementation and timestamp update rules.
Signal and scheduler-entity fields used by adjusted-time normalization and group aggregation locking.

findings.text: Per-CPU usage query returns the stored counter for the requested category, augmented with live pending time when generic virtual timing is active on that CPU, otherwise it delegates to a default helper. When augmentation is active it repeatedly samples the current task under read-side protection and retries on contention until a consistent snapshot is produced.

Whole-CPU snapshot helper copies the base per-CPU table then adds unflushed pending time to a specific category determined by sampled execution state and niceness and waiter presence. Guest execution contributes to guest-specific and corresponding user categories, idle execution splits between idle and wait based on waiters, and sleeping or dead states add nothing. It retries on contention like the per-field query.

Idle and wait microsecond queries are thin wrappers over a shared sleep-time helper, selecting different usage categories and opposite waiter-presence conditions while forwarding the caller timestamp pointer.

User and guest boundary transitions flush pending time for the outgoing mode, update the virtual CPU flag for guest paths, and move the per-task state to the new mode under writer exclusion. Task switch marks the outgoing task inactive and detached, then initializes the incoming task state from its identity as idle, virtual CPU, or regular kernel execution with a fresh start marker and current CPU ownership.

Per-task and thread-group adjusted time queries exist in multiple configurations. A configuration copies stored user and system totals directly, gathering group totals ahead for the group form. Another anchors to scheduler runtime, refreshes user and system portions from live state with fallback to scheduler clock when sampling misses, then normalizes against a previous snapshot to produce monotonic outputs.

Guest time query returns stored guest total plus live pending guest and elapsed portions only when the target is currently in guest execution, observed under reader retry protection; when virtual accounting is disabled it returns the stored total alone.

Periodic tick accounting bails out early for virtual accounting, dynamic-tick idle, or interrupt-time modes. It then subtracts stolen time from tick duration, discards the tick if fully stolen, and otherwise attributes the remainder to user, system, or idle, with idle attribution guarded to exclude the idle task unless interrupt nesting indicates otherwise.

Interrupt-context virtual accounting dispatches by interrupt nesting depth after applying the caller offset. Hard and soft nesting levels each have dedicated handlers, absence of nesting selects between idle-or-kernel attribution and a simple reset depending on dynamic-tick mode and build support for idle virtual accounting.

Elapsed-time helper measures since the stored start marker, subtracts time already accounted elsewhere to avoid negative drift from rounding, advances the start marker by the full elapsed amount, warns if invoked while inactive, and returns only the accountable remainder.
Pending user, system, and guest accumulators retain sub-tick remainders locally and forward to global accounting only upon reaching tick granularity, clearing the local buffer after each forward.

Live sampling is valid only when the observed timing record still belongs to the queried CPU or is detached, and when its state is active rather than mid-switch. User versus nice attribution follows the sign of niceness, guest attribution additionally requires guest state, and idle versus wait attribution follows waiter presence.

Per-task virtual time moves among system, user, guest, idle, and inactive. User entry moves from system to user, user exit returns to system, guest entry and exit toggle the virtual CPU flag while moving between system and guest, and context switch parks the old task as inactive and detached before placing the new task into idle, guest, or system.

Per-task timing record carries a sequence guard for lock-free readers, an execution-state marker, an owning-CPU identifier with a detached sentinel, a start timestamp, and separate pending accumulators for user, system, and guest modes.

Runqueue and domain structures expose current-task pointer, waiter count, online flag, CPU identifier, root-domain pointer, visit cookie, deadline overload count, bandwidth object, and deadline substate with runnable count, earliest deadline, and pushable tree root. Per-CPU tables hold usage counters indexed by usage category.

Current-task sampling holds read-side protection across dereference and sequence-guarded copy, releasing before any backoff and retry. Timing updaters exclude readers with write-side sequence sections while readers retry on concurrent modification. Joint runqueue acquisition requires disabled interrupts, orders locks to avoid deadlock, and reports when the held lock was dropped so callers revalidate migration suitability.

Offline deadline migration transfers bandwidth reservation between runqueues and between root domains while holding the involved runqueues plus each domain bandwidth lock in turn. Tasks that are non-contending or throttled move total and running portions, others move total only, and ownership is then updated to the destination CPU.

Deadline overload is reported as a domain-wide atomic count. Pushable ordering prefers earlier deadlines. A pull is desired only when the queue is online and the previous task belongs to the deadline class. Push and pull work is deferred through per-CPU balance callbacks, with push queued only when pushable entries exist.

Offline migration seeks a locked destination where the task would preempt. After any lock drop it rechecks migration permission, affinity, and queue presence, with extra checks for throttled tasks. If no preemptible target exists it falls back to any active allowed CPU and finally to any active CPU.

Later-CPU search rejects pinned tasks and uninitialized scratch masks, then consults a capacity index for candidate queues with later deadlines. It prefers the last execution CPU for cache affinity, walks wake-affine topology favoring the calling CPU, and otherwise distributes among remaining candidates.

Root-domain visit tracking uses a caller-supplied cookie to ensure each domain is processed idempotently per pass. The initial encounter stores the cookie and reports unvisited, later encounters with the same cookie report visited.
Earliest-deadline test succeeds when the destination has no runnable deadline tasks or when the candidate deadline precedes the stored earliest deadline.

Pushable selection scans the deadline pushable tree in order and returns the initial entry that is neither executing on the queue nor migration-disabled, asserting queue ownership, non-current status, multi-CPU affinity, queued presence, and deadline class.
A joint-lock variant always releases the held runqueue then acquires the ordered pair and reports that the original lock was dropped, requiring callers to revalidate state.

Sampling hazards include a missing current pointer which warns and falls back to unaugmented data, delta computation while inactive which warns, uninitialized candidate masks or pinned affinity which yield no migration target, and failure to find any suitable CPU which warns when admission control is active. Niceness changes between updates can misattribute user versus nice portions.

Deadline period tuning exposes maximum and minimum microsecond controls, defaulting to one [CITED] left-shifted by twenty-two [CITED] (about four [CITED] seconds) and one hundred [CITED], with read-write owner and read-only group and other access [CITED], numeric vector handling with cross-linked bounds so each entry constrains the other, registered under the kernel directory during initialization.
Control names are sched_deadline_period_max_us and sched_deadline_period_min_us, each holding an unsigned integer and sharing a numeric vector handler.
Deadline sysctl table is registered under the kernel hierarchy during early initialization and reports success unconditionally.
